title: Wright Flyer
body:
Wright Flyer was the first powered, heavier-than-air aircraft to make a sustained, controlled flight, flown by the Wright brothers at Kitty Hawk on 17 December 1903. Its first flight lasted twelve seconds and covered thirty-six metres, and it proved that powered flight was possible.

The Wright Flyer is a public fact of world history, and its achievement is commemorated in museums and in the history of every aircraft that followed.

title: Propeller Airliner: Douglas DC-3
body:
Propeller Airliner: Douglas DC-3 entered service in 1936 and became the first airliner that could make money carrying passengers alone. The DC-3's reliability, range, and low operating cost made air travel practical, and thousands were built, many still flying today.

The DC-3 is the classic propeller airliner, and its shape defines the golden age of air travel.

title: Seaplane
body:
Seaplane is an aircraft that takes off from and lands on water, using floats or a boat hull instead of wheels. Seaplanes serve lakes, coasts, and island communities where runways are impractical, and they are used for firefighting, tourism, and remote transport.

Seaplanes keep the romance of early aviation alive, and their water operations are a distinct flying skill.

title: Glider
body:
Glider is an engineless aircraft that flies on rising air — thermals, ridge lift, and waves — staying aloft for hours and travelling hundreds of kilometres without power. Gliders are pure flying, and glider pilots learn energy management that every powered pilot respects.

Gliding is both a sport and a training ground, and its silent flight is the closest flying comes to soaring.

title: Agricultural Plane
body:
Agricultural Plane is a small, rugged aircraft built to spray crops, sow seed, and fight fires from the air, with a hopper for its load and a low, slow flight profile. Agricultural planes work the fields of farming regions worldwide, and they are built to be maintained in the field.

Agricultural planes are working aircraft in the fullest sense, and their pilots fly some of the most demanding low-level work in aviation.

title: Amphibious Plane
body:
Amphibious Plane is an aircraft that can operate from both land and water, with retractable wheels and a boat hull or floats. Amphibious planes serve island resorts, remote lodges, and coastguard work, where the destination may be a runway or a bay.

Amphibious planes are the most versatile small aircraft, and their dual nature makes them favourites for adventure travel.

title: Light Sport Plane
body:
Light Sport Plane is a small, simple aircraft built for recreational flying under light-sport rules, with two seats, modest speed, and economical operation. Light sport planes opened flying to more people by lowering cost and training requirements.

Light sport flying is grassroots aviation, kept alive by clubs, builders, and weekend pilots.

title: Airship and Blimp
body:
Airship and Blimp is a lighter-than-air aircraft lifted by a gas-filled envelope, with engines for propulsion and a gondola for crew and passengers. Airships carried passengers across oceans in the 1930s, and modern blimps serve advertising, surveillance, and tourism roles.

Airships are the gentle giants of aviation history, and their slow, quiet flight still fascinates everyone who sees one.
